source_artifacts.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)

capabilities.target: directory user profile and group memberships
a named user's MFA methods, plus issuance of a temporary access pass

inputs.source: Support ticket submitted through the helpdesk queue, including tickets emailed in by contractors and vendors

instructions.note: The instruction to 'look up the user, reset their MFA' names no restriction tying the target account to the ticket requester's own identity, so any user named in a ticket can be targeted.
'the person who opened the ticket' is treated as equivalent to the account owner with no instruction to verify the two are the same person.

elements.name: External ticket submitter (contractor, vendor, or any email sender)
Temporary pass delivery to ticket requester

controls.name: Service desk analyst approval before MFA reset executes
controls.decay_rationale: Raw-action review by a human does not weaken as the model becomes more capable, but its real-world effectiveness degrades with approval volume (approval fatigue). At roughly 200 requests per analyst per shift, most routine, per-request scrutiny is likely shallow (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Recipient confirmation bound to the account record
controls.decay_rationale: Binding delivery to a verified contact on record is enforced outside the model and does not depend on model capability.

controls.name: Requester-to-account-owner verification before reset
controls.decay_rationale: Verifying the requester against the account's record of ownership is enforced outside the model and does not depend on model capability.

findings.title: Untrusted ticket drives MFA reset and temp-pass delivery to the ticket's own sender, not the account owner (confused deputy, SAFE-T1307)

attack_path.note: An external party (contractor, vendor, or anyone who can email the queue) opens a ticket naming a target user; the 'requester' is just the email sender field, unauthenticated against the target account's ownership.
Agent looks up the named target user's directory profile to action the ticket.
Agent resets the named user's MFA and issues a temporary access pass, gated only by analyst approval.
Agent sends the new temporary pass to the ticket opener (the untrusted requester), not to the verified account owner.

forecast.watch_signal: The approval gate on idp.reset_mfa / chat.send_temp_pass is removed, bypassed for tickets flagged 'routine', or autonomy is raised beyond A2 without a new review.

evidence.observation: "The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner."
"Contractors and vendors can email tickets in. The requester field is the email sender." An email sender field is not verified against the target account's ownership.
The agent looks up the named user, resets their MFA, and sends the temp pass to the ticket opener, with no instruction to verify the opener is the account owner.

evidence.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)
evidence.observation: The queue shows Target, Requested by, and full ticket text (raw_action review), but Requested by is the same unverified email sender field; catching a mismatch depends entirely on analyst attention.

"Two analysts cover the queue and approve about 400 requests per shift; most are routine." About 200 approvals per analyst per shift is high volume, consistent with approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403, ASI09).

recommendations.action: Bind the temporary access pass delivery address to the account owner's verified contact method on record (registered phone or email in the IdP/HR system), never to the free-text ticket requester field.

Require verification that the ticket requester is the account owner (or has documented standing to request a reset for that account), such as a callback to a number on file or manager attestation, before idp.reset_mfa executes.
Automatically flag and route to a second reviewer any ticket where the stated requester does not match the target account's owner of record.
Reduce the number of resets each analyst reviews per shift, or add automated pre-screening, so high-volume routine approval does not degrade into rubber-stamping.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe how the agent authenticates itself to idp.reset_mfa, idp.read_user, or chat.send_temp_pass, so spoofing of the agent's own service identity cannot be assessed.
No information is given on whether the agent's system prompt or tool bindings can be modified without a review process.
Artifacts describe the approval request record but not whether execution of the reset and the temp-pass send are separately logged as an attributable record.
The agent discloses a freshly issued credential (the temp pass) to the ticket's unverified requester rather than the account owner.
Each reset requires individual analyst approval before executing, and no unbounded autonomous loop or spend capability is described for the agent itself.
An external, low-trust requester can cause a privileged credential action (MFA reset) on an arbitrary account, a confused-deputy elevation.
The full ticket body is trusted as the basis for selecting the target account and requester with no integrity check against a system of record.
No information on whether inbound ticket content, which may include PII, is restricted to authorized viewers once ingested.
Artifacts do not state whether ticket submission is rate limited, so flooding-driven approval fatigue beyond the stated 400/shift baseline cannot be assessed.
The requester field is just the email sender, which email alone does not strongly authenticate.
Because the requester identity is only an email sender address, the true originator of a malicious reset request is weakly attributable.
No information on whether the temp-pass message can be altered in transit between the agent and the chat delivery channel.
The core disclosure: the temp pass is delivered to the ticket opener rather than the verified account owner.
A single credential delivery message does not consume resources in a way that enables denial of service.
No information on whether approval decisions or queue entries can be altered after the fact.
The queue is accessible only to service desk analysts per the design description; no separate disclosure path beyond the analyst's intended review is described.
Artifacts do not describe whether the approval queue system itself has throughput limits or could be flooded beyond the stated 400/shift baseline.
The queue records which analyst approved or rejected each named action, target, and requester.
No information on write-protection for directory records that cap.user_read and cap.mfa_reset depend on.
Artifacts do not describe access controls on the identity directory beyond the read capability already modeled as cap.user_read.
A single directory read per ticket does not create a resource exhaustion risk for the identity store.

rating.rationale: One finding (F1) spans the design: an untrusted ticket, including ones emailed in by any outside party, can drive an MFA reset of an arbitrary named user and have the resulting temporary access pass delivered to the ticket's own submitter rather than the verified account owner (SAFE-T1307 confused deputy). With no controls this is a one-step path from an untrusted source to a severe sink (credential_access plus restricted-data egress), so inherent is critical. The only control is a raw-action analyst approval gate, which earns the credit raw-action review allows, but the design states roughly 200 approvals per analyst per shift, mostly routine, which is high volume rather than low; that caps the credit at one tier instead of two and keeps residual at high rather than at or below moderate. No structural control binds the reset target or the pass destination to the account's verified record of ownership, so if the approval gate is weakened or removed (autonomy_increase, control_removal), the forecast reverts to critical. Adding recipient confirmation bound to the record and requester-to-owner verification are the only changes that would sever this path (rubric section 5 step 1).

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No MCP or tool manifest, IaC, or source code was provided; capability scope for idp.reset_mfa, idp.read_user, and chat.send_temp_pass is inferred from prose descriptions, so credential_scope values are marked unknown or best-estimate.
No information was provided on how the agent authenticates to the identity provider tools, so spoofing risk to the agent's own service identity could not be assessed.
No information on email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) for inbound tickets was provided, so the ease of spoofing the requester field is inferred rather than confirmed.
